catalog_citation: Garba, Patience Ashesla & Friday Nyizo Dansabo. 2026. Compound words and phrases distinction in Eggon: a morphosyntactic study. Sokoto Journal of Linguistics and Communication Studies (SOJOLICS) 2(2): 15-29. doi:10.36349/sojolics.2026.v02i02.002
catalog_locator: p.17, sect. 2.1 'Distinguishing Between Compounds and Phrases', final paragraph (deciding sentence); tone statement p.16, sect. 1 Introduction; echoed p.24 (p.10, sect. 4.2) and p.27 (p.13, sect. 5).
catalog_quote: [p.16] The language is tonal with three level tones (high ՛, mid and low ̀). In this article, the high and low tones are marked while the mid tone is unmarked. [...] [p.17] The use of stress to distinguish compounds and phrases as suggested by Booij (2005) and Giegerich (2005) is limited to English and other languages that are intonational. But in tonal languages like Eggon, stress does not exist and cannot distinguish words and phrases. [...] [p.24] Nonetheless, stress alone is not sufficient in distinguishing compounds from phrases but can be used alongside other criteria. This, however, may not apply to some languages that do not make use of stress to distinguish words and phrases such as Eggon. Even though Eggon makes use of tone, it does not distinguish words and phrases. [...] [p.27] the present study shows that phonologically, stress may demarcate compounds from phrases in English, but tone does not distinguish between the two in Eggon.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Eggon is described as a tone language with three level tones (H, M, L; rare contours); the (native-speaker) author asserts that stress does not exist in Eggon and plays no role in distinguishing compounds from phrases. No positive statement of any word-level prominence position exists in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the statement is a blanket assertion made in passing within a morphosyntactic study, not the result of a prosodic analysis
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns the absence of stress generally and specifically as a compound-vs-phrase diagnostic (word/phrase level). The only dedicated phonological description (Sibomana 1985, Kagbu dialect) was not accessible, and Blench's 2015 dictionary introduction (based on Sibomana) describes tones only and is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Garba & Dansabo 2026 describe Eggon generally (first author a native speaker, Nasarawa State University Keffi; dialect not specified). Sibomana 1985 (unseen) focuses on the Kagbu dialect; Mwanti & Alagbe 2025 describe the Wana dialect. All are eggo1239; Glottolog lists no sub-dialect codes used here.

tone_statements.quote: There are two commonly marked tones in Éggὸn: The high ( ́ ) tone and the low ( ̀ ) tone. The mid-tone is not usually marked. There are also falling (˄) and rising (˅) tones (Blench 2006). However, these are not common. Thus, the present study limits itself to the level of tones. The tone in Éggὸn performs both lexical and grammatical functions. … There are thirty-one consonants, seven vowels, and three-level tones which distinguish individual words or perform grammatical functions.
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones, high, mid and low (H and L marked, M unmarked), with lexical and grammatical functions; falling and rising tones reported after Blench 2006 but 'not common'; no word stress.

sources.citation: Garba, Patience Ashesla. 2017. Eggon language counting system and derivational processes. JOLAN: Journal of the Linguistic Association of Nigeria 20(2): 269-275.
sources.tag: read: states tone
sources.quote: There is a null multiplication marker; however, a tone change from low to high shows multiplication. [p.271] ... However, there is no clear plurality marker but there is a change in tone from low tone to high tone. Similarly, èzbihà '2000' is 1000 times two, and there is also no plural marker. In cases where there is no change in vowel, as in, ènd'gàhà '200', èzbíha '2000', there is a slight change in tone from low to high which is used and understood by the speakers to mean multipication. [p.272]
sources.note: Numerals paper with fully tone-marked data (grave = low, acute = high on àkyèn, àhà, èk'pò, ènd'gà, èzbì etc.); its one analytic tone claim is grammatical: multiplication in derived hundreds/thousands has no segmental marker and is signalled by a low-to-high tone change on the base (ènd'gà '100' -> ènd'gáfi '600'; èzbì -> èzbíha '2000'); 'tone change' is listed among the phonological processes of numeral derivation, details deferred to later work. No statement of the tone inventory.
sources.venue: JOLAN: Journal of the Linguistic Association of Nigeria
